note: Seven explicit validation steps including data safety and explainability, which is close to an audit checklist for precision oncology.
title: A framework for validating AI in precision medicine: considerations from the European ITFoC consortium
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making

reading.body:
A 2021 European framework for validating AI in precision medicine sets out seven explicit checks, including data safety and explainability, and has drawn 105 citations.

The seven steps cover intended use, the patients it applies to, when it is tested, which data sets are used, how data quality, privacy and security are handled, how performance is measured, and whether the model can explain its reasoning. That sequence is close to an audit checklist, and it treats explanation as a validation requirement rather than a feature added later. The framework also underpins a challenge platform that compares algorithms on outside data, which tests whether a model holds up beyond the data it was trained on.

The clinical setting matters for how the checks are read. The work centers on triple negative breast cancer and treatment response prediction, drawing on routine care data plus molecular omics held in clinical repositories and biobanks. Models built on that kind of data are only as good as the records and specimens behind them, so data quality, privacy and security are not administrative steps but conditions on whether the model can be trusted at all. The framework is a governance artifact, not a compute or power measurement, and it says nothing about the infrastructure those models run on.

What the data does not cover is how the framework performs in practice. There is no count of institutions that adopted it, no result from the challenge comparison, and no evidence that following the seven steps improves patient outcomes. The citation count shows the paper is referenced, not that its checklist is used. The framework is also specific to precision oncology, so its transfer to other clinical AI is untested here.

explain_beginner: A European group called ITFoC proposed a way to check artificial intelligence used in cancer care. Their focus is a type of breast cancer called triple negative, where the goal is to forecast how someone responds to treatment. The group lists seven checks. These cover what the AI is meant to do, which patients it applies to, when it is tested, which data sets are used, how data quality, privacy and security are handled, how well it performs, and whether its reasoning can be explained. It also supports a contest comparing algorithms on outside data. This matters because AI should be safe, unbiased and transparent before healthcare use.
explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that AI in cancer care should not be adopted without strong validation. The ITFoC consortium created a seven step framework for checking AI that forecasts treatment response, using triple negative breast cancer as the focus. The steps cover what the AI is for, which patients it targets, when it is evaluated, which data sets are used, how data quality, privacy and security are protected, how performance is measured, and whether the AI can explain its reasoning. It also supports a contest platform that compares algorithms on outside data. Decision is to require robust, unbiased and transparent evidence of safety and performance before deploying tools.
explain_practitioner: The ITFoC consortium designed a process to assess AI that forecasts how cancer patients respond to treatment. The work centers on triple negative breast cancer and draws on data from routine care plus molecular omics information held in clinical repositories and biobanks. The process has seven parts. They address what the AI is for, which patients it targets, when it should be evaluated, which data sets are used, how data quality, privacy and security are protected, how performance is measured, and how the AI's reasoning can be explained. It underpins a platform for the ITFoC Challenge, a community competition that will compare algorithms on outside data. This yields structured validation.
